<description>
This migrates the headers presync parameters (`commitment_period` and `redownload_buffer_size`) from being precomputed chainparams to being computed at runtime whenever a headers sync starts. This has as advantages:
* Less work for maintainers that need to occasionally run the current `contrib/devtools/headerssync-params.py` script.
* Less room for mistakes in that process.
* Automatically adapts based on time (as opposed to needing to predict the lifetime of the software).

To achieve this, the parameter search algorithm is implemented in C++. It is simpler, because it does not attempt to model the fact that the attacker is forced to submit their headers in batches of 2000 if they want to maintain the attack. The old Python code did that, but actually got it (slightly) wrong by missing the fact that attackers are capable of strategically deciding to stop the attack in the middle of a batch (found by darosior).

Unit tests and fuzz tests are added, and at the end the old Python code is deleted.
</description>

<commits>
3ddc510850 headerssync: add computation of optimal sync parameters

Add ComputeHeadersSyncParams(), which finds (near-)optimal commitment
period and redownload buffer size values for the headers sync
DoS-protection mechanism, given the timespan since genesis and the
number of headers in the minimum-chainwork chain, along with the
internal ComputeHeadersSyncParamsInner() it is based on.

The attack model treats headers as arriving one at a time, which
slightly overestimates what an attacker can achieve (in reality headers
arrive in batches that are only accepted in their entirety), but leads
to a closed-form expression for the expected number of accepted forged
headers. That expression can be inverted, which gives the buffer size
needed for a given period directly, so only the period is searched for:
by bisecting the legal range for the two adjacent periods which straddle
the optimum of the problem's continuous relaxation, and comparing those
two. If that optimum lies outside the legal range, the two periods
nearest the corresponding end are compared instead.

Also widen next_height in the presync header validation to int64_t,
matching the m_current_height it is computed from. A presync chain is
only bounded by 6 headers per second since genesis, so it can exceed
INT_MAX headers, which the implicit truncation would turn into a
negative height.

The unit test checks 50 inputs against their exact optima, found by an
exhaustive search over all periods. The script which samples such inputs
and computes their optima is included with the test records.

7281e51459 fuzz: add headers sync parameter computation targets

Add two fuzz targets covering the headers sync parameter optimizer over
a broad range of legal inputs, asserting that the resulting
configuration is sane (and, implicitly, that the computation terminates
without crashing or throwing):

- headers_sync_params_inner exercises ComputeHeadersSyncParamsInner
  directly. minchainwork_headers is a block height and thus fits an int;
  max_headers must exceed twice that (which the caller guarantees by
  clamping) and is at most 6 headers/s over the longest timespan that
  std::chrono::seconds is guaranteed to represent; attack_headers is a
  positive rate, parametrized logarithmically over a wide range of
  magnitudes.

- headers_sync_params exercises ComputeHeadersSyncParams over the
  portable range of std::chrono::seconds, and any int-height
  minchainwork_headers.

Both targets check that the returned period is positive and no larger
than the minimum-chainwork chain, and that the redownload buffer covers
at least one commitment period whenever the acceptable attack rate is
low enough to require any commitment verification at all (which it
always is for the rates ComputeHeadersSyncParams uses).

990b3fa6d0 net_processing: compute headers sync parameters at runtime

So far, the headers sync parameters are committed to the repository,
as part of the chain parameters. This requires maintainers to
occasionally recompute them, based on a prediction of how long the
release is likely to be used.

With the optimization algorithm now available in headerssync.cpp, it
becomes possible to instead do this computation at runtime. This is
less work, with fewer ways for maintainers and reviewers to get it
wrong, and automatically adjusts based on clock time.

The computation takes well under a microsecond, so it is simply redone
whenever a headers sync is started. Doing it there, rather than once at
startup, keeps the commitment period consistent with the bound that
HeadersSyncState derives from the clock on how many commitments a peer
may make us store: a node which starts up with a badly wrong clock and
has it corrected before syncing would otherwise use a period sized for
a much shorter chain than a peer can then feed it, inflating that bound
(by a factor 50 for a clock which starts out before genesis). The fuzz
targets which reach this code fix the clock around message processing,
so the parameters they end up with do not vary with the fuzz input.

As the chain parameters no longer hold them, HeadersSyncParams moves to
headerssync.h, next to the code which computes and consumes it.

Co-Authored-By: Lőrinc <pap.lorinc@gmail.com>

4c04debcd7 contrib: remove headerssync-params.py

The headers sync parameters are now computed at runtime, so the tool
that used to generate them for chainparams.cpp has no purpose anymore.

0316d0dc9e test: verify the sync parameters by brute force

The test vectors compare against values obtained by a separate
exhaustive search, so they detect changes in behavior, but not a mistake
in that search. Establish instead, for each of them, that the
configuration really is the one with the lowest memory usage, by
evaluating the attack rate for every integer period, and for every
integer bufsize up to the point where it becomes acceptable. Periods
whose redownload buffer alone outweighs the best configuration found so
far are ruled out by a bound rather than tried, which keeps the search
over the recorded chain lengths affordable.

The recorded bufsize is in addition held against the attack model
itself, by averaging the accepted headers over the offset at which the
attacker's first commitment check falls, instead of against the closed
form that model is condensed into and inverted.

Co-Authored-By: Lőrinc <pap.lorinc@gmail.com>
</commits>

+/** Maximum timespan that the headers sync parameter computation can be asked about.
+ *  std::chrono::seconds is only guaranteed to be a signed integer type of at least 35 bits. */
+constexpr int64_t MAX_TIMESPAN = (int64_t{1} << 34) - 1;
+
+/** The largest max_headers value ComputeHeadersSyncParams can pass to the optimizer. */
+constexpr int64_t MAX_MAX_HEADERS = 6 * MAX_TIMESPAN;

+FUZZ_TARGET(headers_sync_params_inner)
+{
+    FuzzedDataProvider provider(buffer.data(), buffer.size());
+
+    // The number of headers in the minimum-chainwork chain is a block height, so any legal value
+    // fits in an int (see Consensus::Params::minchainwork_height).
+    auto minchainwork_headers = provider.ConsumeIntegralInRange<int64_t>(1, std::numeric_limits<int>::max());
+    // The optimizer requires max_headers > 2 * minchainwork_headers.
+    auto max_headers = provider.ConsumeIntegralInRange<int64_t>(2 * minchainwork_headers + 1, MAX_MAX_HEADERS);
+    // Any positive acceptable attack rate is legal. Parametrize it logarithmically, as the number

+/** Compute the expected number of forged headers an attacker can get accepted per attack.
+ *
+ * This is a naive implementation that computes the expected value by averaging over all possible
+ * values of the offset. See the comment on real_bufsize inside ComputeHeadersSyncParamsInner in
+ * headerssync.cpp.
+ */
+double AttackRateNaive(int64_t period, int64_t bufsize)
+{
+    double accepted{0};
+    for (int64_t offset = 0; offset < period; ++offset) {
+        const int64_t c = (bufsize - offset + period - 1) / period;
+        accepted += std::ldexp(offset + period * c - bufsize + period, -int(c));
+    }
+    return accepted / period;
+}
+
+/** Compute the expected number of forged headers an attacker can get accepted per attack.
+ *
+ * This uses the efficient closed-form expression derived in the comment on real_bufsize inside
+ * ComputeHeadersSyncParamsInner in headerssync.cpp.
+ */
+double AttackRate(int64_t period, int64_t bufsize) noexcept
+{
+    const int64_t k = bufsize / period;
+    const int64_t m = bufsize % period;
+    /** Expected accepted headers, given the first k checks pass. */
+    const double expected_headers = (period * (6.0 * period - 4.0 * m - 2.0) + m * (m + 1.0)) / (4.0 * period);
+    return std::ldexp(expected_headers, -int(k));
+}

+/** Verify by brute force and mild heuristics that a (period, bufsize) configuration really is the
+ *  memory optimum. */
+void CheckOptimal(int64_t max_headers, int64_t minchainwork_headers, double attack_headers,
+                  int64_t expected_period, int64_t expected_bufsize)
+{
+    constexpr int64_t COMPACT_HEADER_SIZE = sizeof(CompressedHeader) * 8;
+    /** The best (period, bufsize, memory) solution so far. */
+    std::optional<std::tuple<int64_t, int64_t, int64_t>> best;
+    int64_t bufsize = 1;
+    for (int64_t period = 1; period <= minchainwork_headers; ++period) {
+        // Stop when the minimum amount of memory just due to the redownload buffer at this period
+        // is already more than the best so far. Larger periods can only increase it further, as the
+        // bound below grows with the period wherever it is positive.
+        //
+        // The formula is a lower bound on the bufsize every acceptable solution at this period
+        // needs. The attack rate always exceeds 2^-floor(bufsize/period) * (3*period - 1) / 4 (see
+        // the bounds on the attack rate in headerssync.cpp), and the floor is at most
+        // bufsize/period.
+        const double min_bufsize = period * std::log2((3.0 * period - 1.0) / (4.0 * attack_headers));
+        if (best.has_value() && min_bufsize * COMPACT_HEADER_SIZE > std::get<2>(*best)) break;
+        // Find the lowest bufsize at this period with acceptable attack rate. The efficient formula
+        // is used here, as the naive one would be far too slow.
+        while (AttackRate(period, bufsize) >= attack_headers) ++bufsize;
+        // In the loop above, we reuse the previous period's bufsize as starting point because the
+        // attack rate at a fixed bufsize never decreases as the period grows. Verify that by
+        // checking that {bufsize - 1, bufsize} is indeed the boundary for acceptable attack rate
+        // (for bufsize 1 that means an empty buffer, which is never acceptable).
+        BOOST_CHECK_GE(AttackRate(period, bufsize - 1), attack_headers);
+        // Compute the exact memory usage, and remember the best one.
+        const int64_t mem = std::max(max_headers / period, minchainwork_headers / period + bufsize * COMPACT_HEADER_SIZE);
+        if (!best.has_value() || mem < std::get<2>(*best)) best = {period, bufsize, mem};
+    }
+    BOOST_CHECK_EQUAL(expected_period, std::get<0>(*best));
+    BOOST_CHECK_EQUAL(expected_bufsize, std::get<1>(*best));
+    // Verify that the found optimal bufsize is indeed at the boundary for its period, using the
+    // naive attack rate implementation (unlike the loop above, which uses the closed-form formula).
+    BOOST_CHECK_LT(AttackRateNaive(expected_period, expected_bufsize), attack_headers);
+    BOOST_CHECK_GE(AttackRateNaive(expected_period, expected_bufsize - 1), attack_headers);
